title: Working-class identity spans income and education groups while carrying a strong partisan and financial-stress pattern
source_unit: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey and linked occupation context

denominator.unit: percent of US adults in Pew survey; respondents saying the term describes them extremely or very well

working_class_2026.unit: percent saying working class describes them well

working_class_2024.unit: percent saying working class describes them well

observations.method: Pew American Trends Panel descriptive comparison across survey waves; self-identification is retained separately from income, education, occupation, and financial-stress variables.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is repeated cross-sectional, not a same-person identity transition. Wording, political context, sample composition, and the meaning of working class can affect responses.
observations.subgroup: US adults; subgroup estimates are reported by income, education, party, race/ethnicity, occupation, and financial stress.
observations.counterinterpretation: A rise in self-identification may reflect changing political language or status meaning rather than worsening material position or occupational change.

observations.period: January 20-26, 2026; working-class identity by party, income, education, and financial stress

denominator.unit: percent within Pew US adult subgroup; self-identification response

republican_or_leaner.unit: percent saying working class describes them well

observations.method: Pew subgroup cross-tabulation; family income tiers use adjusted 2024 earnings and financial-stress categories are source-defined composites.
observations.uncertainty: Subgroup contrasts are descriptive and overlap across dimensions. Party, income, education, financial stress, race, age, and work type are jointly structured; the report's multivariate analysis does not turn identity into a causal outcome.
observations.subgroup: Party, education, income, and financial-stress groups as defined by Pew; subgroup margins and small-cell caveats remain source-specific.
observations.counterinterpretation: Working-class identity is not a direct proxy for low income, material hardship, blue-collar work, or political ideology; many respondents with comfortable finances adopt the label.

observations.period: January 20-26, 2026; working-class identity by work type

denominator.unit: percent within Pew worker subgroup; blue-collar definition combines physical/manual work with selected industrial sectors

blue_collar_workers.unit: percent saying working class describes them well

observations.method: Pew links January 2026 identity responses to occupation and physical-labor information collected in an October 2024 American Trends Panel survey; blue-collar is source-defined.
observations.uncertainty: The linked occupation context is not a current employment trajectory or panel of identity change. The category includes selected sectors and manual/physical work and should not be generalized to all workers or job quality.
observations.subgroup: Blue-collar workers as defined by Pew versus all other workers.
observations.counterinterpretation: The 16-point contrast does not establish that occupation causes identity; status, culture, party, education, financial stress, and perceived social respect may all contribute.

related_sources.claim: Pew's prior work provides occupational and workplace-identity context for the current self-classification layer.
Pew current economic evaluations provide a separate material and political-judgment context.

boundary: This record measures self-identified working-class status and descriptive subgroup associations. It does not measure objective class position, income mobility, occupation quality, material hardship, class consciousness, voting, policy preference, or causal political identity formation.
